about.title: About Me
about.subtitle: Software engineer with a hands-on IT streak
about.description1: Hi, I'm Raul. I graduated from Simon Fraser University with a Bachelor of Applied Science in Computing Science, and I split my time between writing code, running systems, and troubleshooting whatever needs to keep moving. I have shipped React and React Native apps to real users, deployed to AWS, and I built my own high-performance Windows 11 workstation from scratch as part of my CompTIA A+ Core 1 study.
about.description2: My favorite kind of engineering is the kind that actually reaches people. That means writing clean code, but it also means reading error logs at midnight, walking a non-technical user through a fix, tuning BIOS settings until the driver stops crashing, and setting up backup workflows that stop being an afterthought. I like the full loop, not just the fun parts.
about.description3: I studied Computing Science, but I stayed close to the metal. I am fluent with Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, C++, and SQL, and I move comfortably between Windows and Linux, VMware and VirtualBox, AWS and GitHub. Trilingual (English, French, Spanish), based in Vancouver, ready for hybrid work.

rig.title: The Rig
rig.subtitle: ARMOURY Vanguard I-358 — my daily workstation. Every part chosen on purpose.

story.title: Why this build
story.text: I wanted a workstation that could do everything I actually care about: compile code, run several virtual machines at once, play with local LLMs and TensorFlow, encode video, host game dev experiments, and yes — game. And I wanted to do it hands-on: pick every part, understand what each one does, and know how to service it when something goes wrong. This build is my daily driver, my CompTIA A+ practice lab, and the machine I ran my hackathon projects on. Every component below was chosen for a reason. Click any card to see why.
story.clickPrompt: Click any component for the full reasoning

cpu.whyShort: Newest-gen Arrow Lake. Enough cores to run VMs, IDEs, and ML at the same time without choking.
whyLong: Latest-generation Intel Arrow Lake architecture — a real upgrade path over previous Core i7 generations.
20 cores (8 Performance + 12 Efficient) let me run several VMs, an IDE, browsers, and a dev server side by side.
The K suffix means it's unlocked — I can practice CPU tuning as part of my CompTIA A+ hands-on work.
The F suffix drops the integrated GPU, which trims cost and heat because I have a discrete GPU anyway.
LGA 1851 socket gives me a clean upgrade path to future Intel Core Ultra chips without rebuilding.

gpu.spec: Blackwell architecture · 8GB GDDR7 · DLSS 4 · CUDA for ML
gpu.whyShort: Blackwell + CUDA. Great balance for dev, ML experiments, and 1440p gaming without wasting money on a flagship.
whyLong: Blackwell architecture (RTX 50 series) — the latest NVIDIA silicon at time of build.
CUDA cores matter for the ML side of my work: TensorFlow, PyTorch, and local LLM inference all lean on them.
DLSS 4 makes 1440p high-refresh gaming realistic without stepping up to an RTX 5080 or 5090.
8GB GDDR7 is enough for the models and workloads I actually run — not chasing spec sheet numbers I would not use.
Reasonable power draw pairs cleanly with the 850W PSU and leaves headroom for a future upgrade.

motherboard.spec: B860 chipset · LGA 1851 · DDR5 · MicroATX · Native Wi-Fi 7
motherboard.whyShort: ASUS TUF durability + B860 chipset. The board runs the Core Ultra 200S series stable at stock, which is exactly what my workloads need.
whyLong: ASUS TUF Gaming build quality — military-grade caps, reinforced PCIe slot, and a proven VRM design for sustained loads.
B860 chipset supports the full Intel Core Ultra 200S series on LGA 1851 — perfect fit for my Ultra 7 265KF at stock speed.
Native Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 come built in — no add-in cards eating a PCIe slot.
MicroATX form factor slots cleanly into the CG530 mid-tower without wasting space or airflow.
Smart trade-off: I don't overclock production workloads, so paying for Z890 would have been wasted. B860 leaves budget for cooling, PSU, and case fans that actually help.

ram.spec: Dual channel · Room to grow to 64 or 96 GB
ram.whyShort: 32GB is the sweet spot for running VMs, IDEs, browsers, and Docker without ever hitting swap.
whyLong: 32GB comfortably covers my daily workflow: two VMs, VS Code, several dozen browser tabs, and background Docker containers.
DDR5 memory bandwidth actually matters for compilation and ML data pipelines — real, measurable difference.
Dual-channel configuration to keep memory throughput tight.
Upgrade path to 64GB or 96GB when local LLM work grows past what 32GB can hold.
Configured through XMP / EXPO profiles so I could practice memory tuning as part of CompTIA A+ study.

storage.spec: PCIe Gen 4 · Boot + code + VMs on one drive
storage.whyShort: 2TB NVMe is fast enough that boot, build, and VM I/O never feel like the bottleneck.
whyLong: 2TB is enough for Windows, my dev toolchain, several VM images, my Steam library, and local ML models — without juggling.
NVMe read/write speeds keep boot, project builds, and file transfers snappy.
One clean primary drive to start, with room to add secondary drives later without repartitioning anything.
No moving parts — no risk of HDD spin-up latency or mechanical failure during long training runs.
Enough headroom to keep multiple Windows and Linux VMs live for CompTIA A+ practice.

cooler.spec: Air cooling · Fan curves tuned in BIOS
cooler.whyShort: Air cooling on purpose: no pump, no coolant, nothing that leaks. Simple to service and it holds the thermals I need.
whyLong: The Core Ultra 7 265KF is unlocked and pushes real heat under sustained compile or ML training loads.
A tower air cooler plus the CG530's intake and exhaust fans keeps it inside its thermal envelope.
No pump and no coolant loop means one less failure point in a machine I depend on daily.
Easier to service: clearing dust or reseating the cooler is a 10-minute job, not a rebuild.
Fan curves tuned in the BIOS: nearly silent at idle, ramps only when temps actually justify it.

psu.whyShort: 850W 80+ Gold gives me clean, efficient headroom — enough for a future GPU upgrade without touching the power side.
whyLong: 80+ Gold efficiency — less heat, less wasted power, quieter operation under load.
850W is comfortably above what the current Ultra 7 265KF + RTX 5060 Ti draw, so I have real headroom.
That headroom is deliberate: I can drop in an RTX 5070 Ti or higher later without touching the PSU.
Modular cabling keeps the build clean and airflow predictable inside the CG530.
One of the parts I never want to skimp on — a bad PSU takes everything else down with it.

case.spec: Mid Tower · 7× 120mm ARGB fans · Tempered glass
case.whyShort: Mid-tower with 7 ARGB fans out of the box. Serious airflow, room for upgrades, and it actually looks the part.
whyLong: ARMOURY CG530 mid-tower — the signature Vanguard chassis for this build.
Ships with 7 × 120mm ARGB fans out of the box — front intake, top and rear exhaust already dialed in.
Airflow-first internal layout keeps sustained CPU and GPU thermals in check under real workloads.
Enough clearance for a tall air cooler, a full-size GPU, and any future longer card.
Tempered glass side panel — mostly aesthetic, partly practical (I can spot dust and cable issues at a glance).

wireless.whyShort: Latest Wi-Fi and Bluetooth standards, native to the motherboard. No dongles, no compromises.
whyLong: Wi-Fi 7 for future-proof throughput — 6 GHz band, 320 MHz channels, way beyond what Wi-Fi 6E offered.
Bluetooth 5.4 for reliable, low-latency peripherals (headset, mouse, keyboard, controller).
Native to the motherboard, so no PCIe card or USB dongle wasting a slot.
Good enough that I never actually need to run an Ethernet cable across the room to hit real speeds.
One less thing to troubleshoot when the network acts up — it's just there.

os.whyShort: Pro tier because I actually use the extras: Hyper-V for VMs, BitLocker for encryption, GPO for IT practice.
whyLong: Hyper-V lets me spin up Windows and Linux guests directly without needing VMware or VirtualBox for quick tests.
BitLocker drive encryption — real security practice, not a checkbox I ignore.
Group Policy Editor gives me a proper environment to practice the kind of admin work I'd see in an IT job.
Remote Desktop (RDP) support is much better than Home, which matters when I access this machine from another network.
Sits more naturally alongside the Windows Pro / Enterprise environments most Canadian workplaces run.

details.overview: SecuApp is a mobile app for a real client, with an AWS-hosted backend. I joined as a freelance software engineer and I own feature delivery end to end: React Native on the front, backend adjustments on the server side, and direct communication with the client.
features: Built React Native features that map cleanly to the client's real workflow
Debugged and fixed Excel export failures across different data scenarios
Implemented user account, permissions, and access flows
Coordinated directly with the client for requirements, updates, and timeline
Kept the AWS-hosted backend stable through daily usage
Organized digital storage and reporting outputs used across daily workflows

The app had to stay reliable for daily end-user use, not just demo well
Client is non-technical, so trade-offs had to be explained in plain language

Added defensive checks around user input and file generation paths
Kept weekly updates in plain language so the client could make informed calls

elContador.description: E-commerce site for an accounting services business, delivered end to end: React front-end, AWS deployment (EC2, S3, Route 53, IAM), DNS, and admin workflows.

details.overview: El Contador EC needed a full web presence and had no internal technical team. I designed, built, and deployed the whole thing solo: React front-end, AWS infrastructure, DNS, admin flows, and post-launch support.
features: React front-end with responsive layout and clean component structure
Deployed on AWS EC2 with S3 for static assets and Route 53 for DNS
Configured IAM policies for least-privilege access
Set up custom domain, HTTPS, and email routing
Built admin workflows and permissions for the client to manage the site
Continued support and adjustments after launch

Small budget meant every AWS service had to be justified
solution: Chose EC2 + S3 + Route 53 as the boring, well-documented baseline

Kept the stack simple enough to hand off documentation the client can actually follow

ganpi.title: GANPI — CLI + Gemini API (1st Place, StormHacks 2025)
ganpi.description: Command-line tool that turns plain English into safe shell commands using the Google Gemini API. Written in C++. 1st place at StormHacks 2025.

demo.title: GANPI — try it now
demo.subtitle: Type what you want in plain English. GANPI translates it into a shell command, marks it safe / warn / blocked, and only runs it if you approve.
demo.placeholder: e.g. list all files, find every pdf, how much disk space am I using…
demo.footNote: This sandbox uses the same intent + safety layer that sits in front of Gemini in the real CLI. Dangerous commands like rm -rf, chmod 777, or shutdown are blocked or gated before they ever reach a shell.

details.overview: GANPI is a command-line tool that lets you describe what you want in plain English and returns a safe shell command. Built in 36 hours during StormHacks 2025 with a team of four. Won 1st place.
features: C++ CLI with clean argument parsing and error handling
Integrates the Google Gemini API for natural language understanding
Guards against dangerous commands before they run
Cross-platform build and clear installation instructions
Clear, judge-friendly demo and README
challenges: 36-hour deadline with a four-person team meant coordination mattered as much as code
LLM output had to be filtered so we did not hand users a footgun
Demo had to feel polished, not just working
solution: Defined a minimum demo target on day one and worked backwards from it
Added an allowlist / denylist layer between the model output and the shell
Rehearsed the demo before presenting to judges

React Native UI with real navigation and forms
REST API integration for data persistence
Data modeling designed to grow past hackathon scope

React Native UI had to feel finished, not prototype-ish
Team had to agree on a data model quickly

Local LLM inference for privacy-friendly analysis

biomedicalML.title: Canine X-Ray Classification — Deep Learning (CMPT 340)
biomedicalML.description: Group ML project at SFU (CMPT 340 Biomedical Computing). Convolutional neural network trained on veterinary X-ray images of dogs to help flag abnormal findings — a real biomedical imaging pipeline, end to end.

details.overview: Group project for SFU CMPT 340 (Biomedical Computing). We built a deep learning pipeline that takes veterinary X-ray images of dogs and classifies findings the model can support — turning what is usually a slow, expert-only screening task into something that can pre-flag cases for a vet to review. The project touched every part of the biomedical ML loop: image preprocessing, augmentation, model design, training, evaluation on unseen cases, and honest reporting on where the model was and wasn't reliable.
features: CNN trained on veterinary X-ray images of dogs (custom biomedical dataset)
Image preprocessing pipeline: normalization, resizing, and augmentation (rotation, flip, contrast)
TensorFlow / Keras model with transfer learning from a pretrained CNN backbone
Stratified train / validation / test splits to keep evaluation honest
Confusion matrices, precision/recall, and per-class accuracy reported in the writeup
Reproducible training scripts + documented model card
challenges: Medical imaging datasets are small, imbalanced, and expensive to expand — augmentation had to work harder
Overfitting is the default failure mode with limited data; regularization mattered from day one
Group project meant the pipeline had to be splittable without collisions across four people
details.solution: Locked the image pipeline and data splits early, chose a pretrained CNN backbone to squeeze value out of a small dataset, added aggressive augmentation and dropout to fight overfitting, and split the work along clean boundaries (data pipeline, model, evaluation, report) so every branch could merge without stepping on the others.

mountainMadness.title: Mountain Madness — Chrome Extension + CV
mountainMadness.description: Chrome extension that uses OpenCV and DeepFace for real-time computer vision experiments inside the browser. Python + JavaScript, hackathon project.

details.overview: Mountain Madness is a Chrome extension hackathon project that experiments with running computer vision (OpenCV, DeepFace) tied into the browser context.
features: Chrome Extension API integration
Python + JavaScript pipeline for computer vision tasks
OpenCV for image processing
DeepFace for face analysis
Focused hackathon scope
challenges: Browser extension security model limits what you can run where
Latency between page context and model inference had to feel invisible
details.solution: Split work between what the extension does inline and what happens off-page in a helper process, and kept the UX around a single simple flow so the extension felt purposeful rather than experimental.

tuSalud.title: TuSalud — Patient Support, Records & Report Automation
tuSalud.description: Multi-hat role at a private medical services company: reading patient profiles, front-line customer service in English and Spanish, records management with role-based access, and a Python pipeline that automated the worst manual work in the office.

details.overview: TuSalud is a private medical services company where I wore several hats at once. I read and interpreted patient medical profiles, answered patient inquiries directly, managed digital records with proper role-based access, and — because I'm a developer — built the Python pipeline that automated the most painful part of the job: parsing long medical reports into structured Excel summaries. The role only worked if I could move between people and code without dropping either side.
features: Read and interpreted patient medical profiles: dates, results, reference ranges, and flagged values
Front-line patient support in Spanish and English by phone, WhatsApp, and email
Managed digital records so the right staff saw the right data — records-management discipline, not just file storage
Set up role-based access separating admin, front desk, and clinical views
Built a Python pipeline (pandas + openpyxl) that reads long medical reports and outputs a formatted Excel summary
Consolidated and cross-checked patient data across sources with SQL and pandas
Standardized inconsistent report formats between labs and flagged entries needing manual follow-up
Wrote internal SOPs so the admin team could keep the workflow running without me
challenges: The job was half people, half data — dropping either side broke the whole workflow
Report formats varied between labs, so a naive parser was not enough
Patient data is sensitive: access had to be tightly scoped from day one
Non-technical staff needed a summary they could scan quickly, not a raw data dump
Some patients were anxious or in a hurry — the customer service side had to stay calm and clear
solution: Used pandas for flexible parsing and normalization across every report format we saw
Used openpyxl to produce formatted Excel summaries matching existing office workflows
Locked down access by role from the start rather than opening things up and cleaning later
Kept the patient-facing side warm and plain-language — being technical didn't mean skipping the human side
Validated outputs against manual samples until admins trusted the results
Documented the pipeline so the team could rerun it on any new batch without asking me

details.overview: ARMOURY Vanguard I-358 is my daily workstation. I picked each part on purpose: enough headroom for code, VMs, and ML experiments, quiet enough to sit next to me for 12-hour dev sessions, and enough hands-on complexity to double as my CompTIA A+ practice lab. Every card below shows what I chose and why.

comptia.title: CompTIA A+ Core 1 — Self-Study
comptia.description: Actively preparing for the CompTIA A+ Core 1 certification (220-1201). Structured study paired with real hands-on practice on my custom workstation.

details.overview: I'm actively studying for the CompTIA A+ Core 1 exam (220-1201). The goal is to formalize the hardware, networking, mobile devices, virtualization, and troubleshooting knowledge I already use every day. Every domain the exam covers, I get to practice on the real machine sitting on my desk.

domains.body: TCP/IP, DNS, DHCP, common ports and protocols, Wi-Fi standards through Wi-Fi 7, networking hardware and cabling.

domains.title: Hardware

domains.title: Virtualization & Cloud

domains.title: Hardware & Network Troubleshooting
domains.body: Diagnosing failures methodically: verify one component at a time, read the actual logs, prove the fix.

approach: Daily reading and practice questions to lock in the exam-critical facts.
Hands-on practice on my ARMOURY Vanguard PC — every part I studied I can physically point to.
Live labs on VMware and VirtualBox to rehearse OS install, imaging, and network troubleshooting.
Documenting mistakes as I go, the same way I would document a real support ticket.
Cross-referencing exam objectives (220-1201) against real work I've done at TuSalud, SecuApp, and El Contador.

CSV / Excel cleanup and standardization scripts

details.overview: I built this because my ARMOURY Vanguard I-358 workstation runs everything — dev, VMs, ML experiments, games — and I wanted the same visibility over it that a real IT team has over a server. It's a small Python daemon that samples the machine every 5 minutes, writes to SQLite, sends me a weekly PDF digest, and pings me on Discord when a threshold is crossed. Same discipline as a real support monitoring stack, scaled down to one workstation.
features: Samples CPU / GPU temperatures, per-core load, RAM, disk I/O, and fan RPM every 5 minutes
Writes each sample to SQLite so I can query trends weeks later, not just the current moment
Weekly PDF digest with matplotlib charts: idle vs load hours, temp peaks, thermal-throttle events
Threshold-based alerts to Discord webhook when GPU > 82 °C, CPU > 90 °C, or disk usage > 90 %
Runs as a Windows Scheduled Task so it survives reboots without a manual restart
CLI for ad-hoc queries: `watchdog last 24h`, `watchdog peaks month`, `watchdog export csv`
challenges: GPU temperature isn't exposed via psutil on Windows — needed a fallback
Sampling too often would create noise; too rarely would miss short thermal spikes
Alerts had to be useful, not spammy — a single hot minute isn't a problem
The whole thing had to be boring and reliable, not a hobby that stops running after a week
solution: Combined psutil (CPU / RAM / disk / fan) with WMI + NVML for GPU-specific counters on Windows
5-minute sampling with 30-second bursts on demand for troubleshooting sessions
Alerts require a sustained breach (3 samples in a row) before they fire — no single-spike noise
Deployed as a Scheduled Task with a health-check job that pings me if the daemon itself stops
Rotated SQLite database monthly and kept aggregates so long-term storage stays tiny

jarvis.title: Jarvis — Personal AI Assistant (Python, always-on)
jarvis.description: A real Jarvis. Two claps in any room launch him — no keyboard, no terminal. Instead of a console, a translucent circular orb docks itself on the right edge of my screen and reacts in real time to every state: idle, listening, thinking, speaking. He greets me in a neural voice as 'sir', then listens for 'hey jarvis' to take voice commands: news, live soccer scores, system stats, timers, media control, screenshots, jokes — all offline-friendly, no LLM, no API keys.

details.overview: Jarvis is my personal assistant, wired into Windows so it feels closer to Tony Stark's than a chatbot. A background clap watcher (sounddevice + numpy) monitors the mic 24/7 and launches Jarvis when it detects two amplitude spikes 150-1200 ms apart. On boot Jarvis addresses me as 'sir' with a neural voice from Microsoft Edge (edge-tts, 400+ voices), opens Spotify + Google, and drops into a wake-word loop listening for 'hey jarvis'. Every subsystem is offline-first or uses free public APIs — no OpenAI, no Anthropic, no cloud dependency, no API keys.
features: Clap-to-launch: two claps anywhere in the room wake Jarvis even when he's closed (Windows startup service)

Floating orb HUD (PySide6): frameless, translucent, always-on-top circle painted from scratch — radial + conic gradients, rotating dashed arcs, sonar ripples on listen, waveform pulses on speak, spinning loader on think
Wake word 'hey jarvis' with word-boundary matching and inline commands ('hey jarvis, play blinding lights')
Neural voice via edge-tts — Jenny, Aria, Michelle, Sonia, Dalia, Denise, etc. Runtime language toggle EN/ES/FR/UK
'Sir' addressing mode: every response ends with the configured honorific, appended naturally to punctuation
News (Google News RSS, 7 topics + free-form search) — 'news tech', 'what's happening in AI'
Live soccer (ESPN JSON, 12 leagues) — 'scores champions', 'scores la liga', 'scores peru'
System info via psutil — battery, CPU load + GHz, RAM, disk, IP, Wi-Fi SSID + signal
Real audio control — master volume get/set via pycaw (IAudioEndpointVolume), media keys (play/pause/next/prev)
Timers, Pomodoro, and voice reminders on threaded scheduler — 'set a timer for 25 minutes', 'remind me in 30 min to stretch'
Screenshots to Desktop (respects OneDrive redirection), jokes (JokeAPI), trivia (OpenTDB), weather (wttr.in)
Auto-pauses the wake listener while speaking so it doesn't hear itself (250 ms grace period)
challenges: Detecting claps without triggering on speech, keyboard, or music — needed peak + timing + noise-floor filtering
Preventing the wake-word listener from transcribing Jarvis's own TTS output
Concurrent typed + spoken input in wake mode without dropping commands or blocking the audio thread
Neural TTS output is MP3; needed a lightweight in-process player that doesn't spawn extra windows
Preventing duplicate Jarvis instances when the clap watcher is over-eager
Bridging non-Qt background threads (wake listener, TTS engine) into the Qt event loop that paints the HUD
solution: Clap state machine: 'idle' → 'one_clap' → verify 150-1200 ms gap → fire → 3s cooldown. Peak ≥ threshold, RMS < noise-floor between claps
Voice.say() pauses the wake listener via threading.Event before playback, resumes 250 ms after — no feedback loops
queue.Queue between wake listener, stdin thread, and dispatcher — command sources are decoupled from the main loop
pygame.mixer plays edge-tts MP3s in-process. Falls back to SAPI5 Zira / Hazel / Helena if edge-tts is unreachable
PID lock file in %TEMP%; clap watcher checks with OpenProcess before launching. Silent auto-start via .vbs + pythonw.exe
JarvisBridge (QObject) exposes state_changed / transcript signals; background threads emit into them and Qt::QueuedConnection dispatches paint updates onto the GUI thread — thread-safety for free

demo.note: This is a simplified web demo — pattern-matched intents and free public APIs (Open-Meteo for weather, JokeAPI, OpenTDB). The real Jarvis runs locally on Python: neural-voice TTS, always-on wake word, launches Spotify + apps, controls master volume, takes screenshots, and boots with two claps anywhere in the room. Still improving — calendar + email hooks and a full LLM fallback are next.

commonplace.title: Commonplace — ideas from the global canon
commonplace.description: A reading room, not a feed. One claim from a canonical book, the century that made it, a counter-book, and a question you actually answer. What you keep comes back later.

details.overview: Commonplace is a small app for learning from historically and globally recognized books — Gilgamesh to Rawls, the Gita to Achebe — without dumping copyrighted text. Each card is an original thesis: argument, context, a rival book, and a prompt. Paths replace infinite scroll; a local spaced-return shelf brings back what you asked to remember.
features: One idea at a time instead of a snackable infinite feed
Eight human paths: power, the self, knowledge, justice, nature, freedom, God and the void, a people
Chronological shelf of the canon, from cuneiform to the veil of ignorance
You write a one-line answer; it stays in this browser
Kept ideas return in 2, 7, 21 days — a commonplace book, not streaks-for-streaks
Original commentary only: map of the books, not a transcription
challenges: Deepstash-style products optimize for swipe rate; that fights memory
Dumping book text is both illegal and a lazy way to 'teach'
A canon that is only European is not a global canon
solution: Force depth: claim + argument + era + counter-voice + a question you answer
Teach with original commentary and bibliographic pointers, never extracts of the work
Thread Mesopotamia, China, India, the Maghreb, Russia, the Caribbean, Latin America, and the West into the same shelf

faultBench.title: Fault Bench — service bay diagnostics
faultBench.description: LeetCode for IT. CompTIA tracks (A+ Core 1/2, Network+, Security+) plus a General desk. The ticket names a symptom, never a cause. A wrong fix costs hours.

details.overview: Fault Bench is a simulated repair bay for CompTIA-style troubleshooting. Each job is a real-feeling Windows box with one root cause and several red herrings. You pay in labor minutes for every tool you open. Reinstalling Windows is almost never the first move.
features: Exam tracks: A+ Core 1/2, Network+, Security+ (defense only), plus General — original tickets, not dumps
Tools that look like the job: Event Viewer, Device Manager, SMART, sensors, cmd (ipconfig/ping/nslookup), memtest, ATX rails, BIOS
Wrong fixes stay wrong — chkdsk does not save NAND, RMA does not fix Code 43
Labor clock and first-contact-resolution, saved in this browser
Identify → test → plan → implement → verify, as a bench habit, not a quiz stem
challenges: IT study apps default to multiple choice, which trains recognition, not isolation
A symptom like 'no internet' has six plausible layers; the UI has to let you walk OSI without spoiling the answer
Hardware faults need live-feeling numbers or they read as flashcards
solution: Every case hides the cause in a specific tool output and plants a herring in another
A small network terminal: ping 8.8.8.8 vs ping google.com is a lesson you run, not a paragraph you read
Sensors tick, memtest progresses, 12V sags under load — then you pick a fix and live with it
